young.html: Denis Diderot was a French writer who spent twenty-five years making a giant book of everything people knew, the Encyclopedia. He also wrote a funny, strange conversation that he never published.

In it, a thoughtful philosopher called Me meets a man called Him at a café in Paris, where people come to watch chess. Him is the nephew of a famous composer, Rameau. He is clever, a wonderful mimic, and very poor.

Him acts out whole operas by himself, playing every instrument and singing every part, until a crowd gathers. But he also says that being good is foolish and that he would rather flatter rich people for a free dinner. Me tries to argue with him. Who wins? Diderot lets the reader decide.

young.cap: Who said it? Sort each idea to Me (the philosopher) or Him (the nephew).

young.html: Two voices. Pick a question, such as "Is it better to be honest or popular?" One person argues one side as strongly as they can, and the other argues the opposite. Then switch sides! Talk about it: is it easier to argue for what you believe, or against it?

full.text: A dialogue with a strange history

full.html: Diderot (1713–1784) edited the Encyclopédie (1751–1772), a huge work of the French Enlightenment that set out the arts, sciences and trades and was repeatedly banned. He wrote Rameau's Nephew over many years, probably between about 1761 and 1774, and kept it private. It was first published in 1805, in a German translation by Goethe; the French text appeared later, and Diderot's own manuscript turned up in a Paris bookstall in 1890.

About quotations. We could not confirm a public-domain English translation of this work that can be read online, so this rung describes it in our own words and quotes nothing. Look for English translations in a library (see the box at the top of the page).

The narrator, Me (Moi), is a philosopher who believes that virtue and happiness go together. Him (Lui), the nephew of the composer Jean-Philippe Rameau, is a real person whom Diderot knew: talented, penniless, living by entertaining wealthy patrons. In the café de la Régence, by the chess players, they talk for an afternoon about music, education, genius, money and morals.

Him is shameless and brilliant. He says that in a society where everyone flatters the powerful, a man is a fool not to do the same; he describes the "positions" people take, like dancers, to please those above them; and he mocks Me's virtue as a luxury of people who can afford it. Yet he also admits he is unhappy, envies his uncle's genius, and speaks with real grief of his late wife.

The talk often turns into performance. Him mimes a violinist, a harpsichord player, a whole opera house, until the chess players stop to watch. These scenes made the book famous. Diderot also uses them to argue a point he cared about: that the new Italian comic opera, with its natural melody, was better than the stiff French style of the elder Rameau.

full.cap: Sort claims from the dialogue (in our own summaries) to the speaker who makes them.

full.html: A dialogue without a winner. Unlike many philosophical dialogues, this one doesn't end with the wise speaker proving his case. Me gives Him good answers, but Him's attacks are never fully refuted. The reader must weigh them.

Assuming Me speaks for Diderot and Him is simply the villain. Many readers think Diderot put parts of himself into both, including his own doubts about whether a good man can thrive in a corrupt society.

deep.html: Goethe translated it; Hegel, in the next era, used Him as a picture of a mind that sees through every pretense of its society and is torn apart by it, and Marx and Freud admired it too. Readers have seen in the nephew a first portrait of a modern type: the clever outsider who mocks every value but can find none to live by. The book also raises a question the Enlightenment hoped to answer: can reason and virtue make people happy when society rewards flattery?

items: Can a person be very talented and still unhappy? Why?
Is it ever smart to be dishonest? Is it ever right?
Why might a writer let the "wrong" side argue well?

questions: Why do you think Diderot never published this dialogue?
Him says good people are foolish. How would you answer him?
Is it fair to judge someone who flatters others because he is poor and hungry?
What makes a conversation interesting to listen to?
Can you be very good at something and still feel like a failure?
